title: Asynchronous Programming
summary: Callbacks, promises and async/await, plus the event loop that decides what runs next: sync code, then microtasks, then tasks.

lessons.title: Sync vs async, and callbacks
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, apply asynchronous programming concepts.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: JavaScript runs **one job at a time** on one **thread** (one line of work). Slow work, like a timer, a network call or reading a file, does not block it. The engine hands that work off and keeps going. When it finishes, a **callback** (a function you passed in, to be called later) waits in line to run.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A café with one barista. She starts your coffee machine, then serves the next person while it brews. When it beeps, your name goes on a list. Where it stops: she never drops an order halfway to grab a ready coffee. Each job finishes first. That rule is called **run-to-completion**.

cards.title: Sync and async
cards.body: **Synchronous** code runs line by line. Each line waits for the one before. **Asynchronous** code starts now and finishes later. `setTimeout`, `fetch`, browser events and Node file reads are asynchronous. The lines after them run first, before their callbacks.

cards.title: Later means later
cards.body: The timer callback waits until the current code is done, even with a 0 ms delay.

cards.title: Node style: error first
cards.body: This is an **error-first callback**. The first argument is the error, or `null` when all went well. The result comes second. Check `err` first.

cards.title: Callback hell
cards.body: Say each step needs the result of the step before. Then callbacks nest inside callbacks. The code drifts to the right, and you must check errors at every level. People call this **callback hell**. Promises and `async`/`await` were made to flatten it.

"Wrap the call in `try...catch` to catch its errors." Not with callbacks. The `try` block has already finished when the callback runs later. An error thrown inside the callback is not caught there. Handle errors inside the callback, or switch to promises.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Start now, finish later, wait your turn.** An async callback never cuts in front of code that is already running.

terms.say: One line of work a computer does, step by step. Your JavaScript code runs on one main thread, so it does one thing at a time.
A function you hand to another function, so it can call yours later. Like leaving your phone number so the shop can ring you when the order is ready.
The rule that a piece of JavaScript finishes before anything else starts. Nothing jumps in halfway, not even a timer that is due.
Code that runs in order, one line after another. Each line waits until the line before it is done.
Work that starts now and finishes later. Your code keeps going, and a callback or promise handles the result when it is ready.
A built-in function that runs a callback after at least some number of milliseconds. It never runs it before the current code is finished.
Node's callback style. The first thing passed in is the error, or null if all went well. The result comes second.
Callbacks nested inside callbacks inside callbacks. The code drifts right and gets hard to read and to fix.
A block that catches errors thrown inside it, so the program does not crash. It only catches errors thrown while it is running.

lessons.title: Promises: states, then, catch, finally
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, apply asynchronous programming concepts.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **promise** is an object that stands for a result that is not ready yet. Functions like `fetch` hand you one right away. Later it gets a value, or an error. You attach a **handler** (a function to run when it is ready) with `then`.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A buzzer at a burger place. You get it at once, before the food exists. Later it buzzes: order ready, or sorry, sold out. Where it stops: a promise buzzes only once. It can never switch from ready to sold out.

cards.title: Three states
items: **rejected**: failed with a reason, usually an `Error`
Fulfilled or rejected means **settled**. A promise settles once and never changes again.

cards.title: Make one
cards.body: The **executor** (the function you pass to `new Promise`) runs at once. Call `resolve(value)` to fulfill it or `reject(reason)` to reject it.

cards.title: Chains
cards.body: `then` always returns a **new promise**. What your handler returns feeds the next `then`. Return a promise, and the chain waits for it. A thrown error skips ahead to the next `catch`. `catch(fn)` is the same as `then(undefined, fn)`.

cards.title: finally
cards.body: `finally` runs either way, and its callback gets no argument. It passes the earlier value or error along unchanged, unless it throws.

"`then` runs right away if the promise is already fulfilled." No. A `then` handler **always runs later**, as a **microtask** (a small job that waits until the current code is done). Handlers added after the promise settles still run. Also: forget to `return` in `then`, and the next step gets `undefined`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Pending first, settled once, set in stone.** `then` for good news, `catch` for bad news, `finally` for both.

terms.say: An object that stands for a result you will get later. It ends up either with a value or with an error.
A function you give a promise or an event, so it can run when something happens. With promises, you attach it with then or catch.
The first state of a promise: still waiting. It has no value and no error yet.
A promise that finished well. It now holds a value, and its then handlers get that value.
A promise that failed. It now holds a reason, usually an Error, and its catch handlers get it.
Done waiting: either fulfilled or rejected. Once a promise is settled, it can never change again.
The function you pass to new Promise. It runs right away and gets two functions, resolve and reject, to finish the promise.
The function you call inside a new promise to say the work is done. The value you pass becomes the promise result.
A small job that waits until the code running now has finished. Promise handlers are microtasks. They run before timers and clicks.

lessons.title: Promise.all, allSettled, any and race
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, apply asynchronous programming concepts.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Often you start several async jobs at once. The **promise combinators** wait on a whole group and give back one promise. Pick the one that fits: you need every result, every outcome, the first success, or the first to finish.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Friends ordering food. `all`: dinner starts when every dish arrives, and one burnt dish cancels dinner. `allSettled`: you list every dish, good or burnt. `any`: you eat the first good dish. `race`: whatever lands first decides, even a burnt one. Where it stops: nothing really gets **cancelled**. The other dishes still cook.

cards.title: The four
items: `Promise.all`: fulfills with an array of values in **input order**. It rejects as soon as one rejects.
`Promise.allSettled`: always fulfills, with one `{ status, value }` or `{ status, reason }` object per input.
`Promise.any`: fulfills with the first value. It rejects with an `AggregateError` only if all of them reject.
`Promise.race`: settles the same way as the first one to settle.

cards.title: Two requests at once
cards.body: Both requests run at the same time. The results come back in the order you listed them, not the order they finished.

cards.title: Empty input
cards.body: Give them an empty array. `all` and `allSettled` fulfill with `[]`. `any` rejects with an `AggregateError`, because nothing could succeed. `race` stays **pending** forever, because nothing ever settles.

"When `Promise.all` rejects, it stops the other requests." No. A promise cannot be cancelled. The other jobs keep running, and their results are just ignored. Also: `any` skips rejections until all fail, but `race` takes a rejection if it comes first.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **All: every one or bust. AllSettled: the full report card. Any: the first win. Race: the first finish, win or lose.**

terms.say: Helpers like Promise.all that take a list of promises and give back one promise for the whole group.
Waits for every promise in a list. You get all the values in a list, or the first error if any one fails.
Waits for every promise, win or lose. You always get a report: one object per promise saying fulfilled or rejected.
Gives you the first promise that succeeds. It only fails if every single one fails.
Copies whichever promise finishes first, whether it succeeded or failed.
The order you wrote the promises in. Promise.all keeps that order in its results, even if a later one finished first.
An error that holds a list of other errors in its errors property. Promise.any rejects with one when every promise failed.
Still waiting, not finished. A promise from Promise.race with an empty list stays like this forever.
Stopped before it finishes. A plain promise has no cancel button, so its work keeps going even when nobody wants the result.

lessons.title: async and await
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, apply asynchronous programming concepts.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: `async` and `await` let you write promise code that **reads top to bottom**, like normal code. No long `then` chains. Under the hood it is still promises. Every promise rule you know still applies.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A recipe that tells you to wait for the dough to rise. You put that recipe down, do other chores, and later pick it up at the same line. Where it stops: only this one function waits. The rest of the program keeps running.

cards.title: The rules
cards.body: An `async` function **always returns a promise**. Return a value, and the promise fulfills with it. Throw, and the promise rejects. `await` pauses that function until a promise settles, then hands you its value. If the promise rejects, `await` throws the error right there.

cards.title: Catch with try
cards.body: Wrap `await` in `try...catch` to handle a rejected promise like any thrown error.

cards.title: Where await works
cards.body: `await` works inside an `async` function, or at the **top level of a module** (ES2022). In a normal function it is a `SyntaxError`. An `async` callback inside `forEach` does not make `forEach` wait. Use a `for...of` loop instead.

cards.title: One by one, or together
cards.body: Each `await` waits for the one before. To run jobs **in parallel**, start them all, then `await Promise.all`.

"Calling an `async` function gives you its return value." No, it gives you a promise. `const user = getUser()` without `await` holds a promise, not the user. And a rejection nobody awaits or catches becomes an **unhandled rejection**.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Async wraps, await unwraps.** `async` wraps the result in a promise. `await` unwraps a promise back into its value.

terms.say: A word you put before a function. It makes the function always return a promise and lets you use await inside it.
Pauses an async function until a promise is done, then gives you its value. Other code keeps running while it waits.
Code in a module file that is not inside any function. Since ES2022 you can use await there.
An error for code the engine cannot even read, like a word in the wrong place. The code never starts running.
An array method that calls a function once per item. It never waits for promises, so it does not work with await.
A loop that goes through the items of an array one by one. Inside an async function, an await in it really waits each time.
At the same time, side by side. Start several jobs, then wait for all of them together.
A promise that failed while nobody was listening with catch or await. Browsers log it, and Node.js stops the program by default.
A block that catches errors thrown inside it. With await, a rejected promise counts as a thrown error, so catch gets it.

lessons.title: The event loop: microtasks before tasks
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, use event loop and event monitor or determine loop outcomes.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The **event loop** decides what runs next. JavaScript has a **call stack** (the functions running right now) and queues of waiting callbacks. When the stack is empty, the loop picks the next waiting job. Which queue it picks from decides what you see logged.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A ride with a VIP line. The ride takes one group at a time. Before each normal group, every VIP gets on, even VIPs who arrive while others board. VIPs are microtasks; the normal line is tasks. Where it stops: the VIP line has no limit, so it can block everyone else.

cards.title: Two queues
items: **Tasks** (also called macrotasks): `setTimeout` and `setInterval` callbacks, events like clicks, I/O callbacks
**Microtasks**: promise handlers (`then`, `catch`, `finally`), code after `await`, `queueMicrotask` callbacks, `MutationObserver` callbacks

cards.title: The order
items: 1. All **synchronous** code runs to the end.
2. **All** microtasks run, even new ones added along the way.
4. All microtasks again, then the next task, and so on.

cards.title: See it
cards.body: Sync code first, then the microtask, then the timer task, even though the timer was set first.

cards.title: Watch events live
cards.body: In the Chrome DevTools console, `monitorEvents(object, events)` logs each matching event as it happens. Try `monitorEvents($0, 'click')`, where `$0` is the element you selected. `unmonitorEvents(object)` stops it. It is a quick **event monitor** that needs no code changes.

"`setTimeout(fn, 0)` beats a promise because it was set first." No. Set-up order only matters inside one queue. The microtask queue is **always emptied first**. A microtask that keeps adding microtasks can **starve** the page: timers and clicks never get a turn.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Sync, then all the micro, then one macro.** Repeat.

terms.say: The part of JavaScript that keeps picking the next job to run. When the running code is done, it takes a waiting callback from a queue.
The pile of functions running right now. A called function goes on top and comes off when it returns.
Bigger waiting jobs, like timer callbacks and clicks. The event loop runs just one, then empties the microtask line again.
Small jobs, like promise handlers. They all run as soon as the current code ends, before any timer or click.
A built-in function that runs a callback again and again, waiting at least the given milliseconds between runs.
A built-in function that adds your callback to the microtask line, the same line promise handlers use.
A browser tool that tells you when part of the page changes. Its callback runs as a microtask.
A Chrome DevTools console helper. It prints each event of the kinds you name on an element, until you stop it.
To keep something from ever getting a turn. Endless microtasks starve timers, clicks and screen updates.

lessons.title: Predicting the output: timers, loops and order
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, use event loop and event monitor or determine loop outcomes.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Exam questions love "What is logged?" Work it out with a routine, not a guess. Sort each log into **sync**, **microtask** or **task**. Then read them out in that order. A few special cases change where a line lands.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Sorting mail into three trays: now, next and later. Read the code top to bottom and drop each log into its tray. Then empty the trays in order. Where it stops: a callback can add new mail when it runs, so keep sorting as you go.

cards.title: Where lines land
items: The `new Promise` **executor** body: sync, it runs at once
Code before the first `await` in an `async` function: sync
`setTimeout(fn, 0)`: a task. 0 is a **minimum delay**, not "right now".

cards.title: The loop trap
cards.body: `var` makes one shared `i`, and it is already 3 when the timers run. `let` makes a fresh `i` for each turn, so each callback keeps its own.

cards.title: Executor is sync
cards.body: C is inside the executor, so it is sync. D is a microtask. B is a task, so it comes last.

cards.title: Node.js extras
cards.body: In Node, `process.nextTick` callbacks run before promise handlers in a **CommonJS** script, and before the loop moves on. `setImmediate` runs in the **check phase**, after I/O. In the main script, `setTimeout(0)` vs `setImmediate` has no fixed order. Inside an I/O callback, `setImmediate` always goes first.

"A 20 ms timer set first runs before a 0 ms timer set second." No. Timers run when they are due, so the 0 ms one goes first. Another trap: `await` on a plain value still pauses. The rest of the function waits for a microtask.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Now, next, later.** Sync now, microtasks next, tasks later. The executor is now. After `await` is next.

terms.say: A small job, like a promise handler or the code after await. All of them run as soon as the current code ends.
A bigger waiting job, like a timer callback. One runs, then all the microtasks run, then the next task.
The function you pass to new Promise. It runs right away, during the normal code, not later.
The shortest wait, not an exact time. The callback may run later if other code is busy, but never sooner.
The old way to make a variable. In a loop there is only one var variable, shared by every turn.
A Node.js function that runs a callback as soon as the current code ends, even before promise handlers in a CommonJS script.
A Node.js function that runs a callback in the check phase, right after Node looks for finished I/O.
A step of the Node.js event loop that comes right after waiting for I/O. setImmediate callbacks run here.
The classic Node.js module style, with require and module.exports. A plain .js file uses it unless the project says "type": "module".

flashcards.front: What does single-threaded mean for JavaScript?
flashcards.back: Your code runs one piece at a time on one main thread. Slow work like timers and I/O happens outside it, and the callback waits in a queue.
Node's callback style. The first argument is the error, or `null` when it worked. The result comes second. Always check `err` first.

flashcards.front: Why does `try...catch` not catch an error thrown in a `setTimeout` callback?
flashcards.back: The `try` block has already finished when the callback runs later. Handle the error inside the callback, or use promises.

flashcards.front: What are the three states of a promise?
flashcards.back: **Pending** (waiting), **fulfilled** (has a value) and **rejected** (has a reason). Fulfilled or rejected means settled, and a settled promise never changes.
A new promise. It fulfills with what the handler returns. If the handler returns a promise, it waits for it. If the handler throws, it rejects.

flashcards.front: What does `finally` pass down the chain?
flashcards.back: The earlier value or error, unchanged. Its callback gets no argument. Only a throw (or a rejected promise) inside `finally` changes the result.

flashcards.front: Does a promise executor run now or later?
flashcards.back: Now. The function passed to `new Promise` runs at once, as normal sync code. Only the `then` handlers run later.
`all` gives the values in input order, or rejects on the first rejection. `allSettled` always fulfills, with a `{ status, value }` or `{ status, reason }` object for each input.
`any` takes the first success and rejects with an `AggregateError` only if all fail. `race` copies the first to settle, even a rejection.

flashcards.front: What do the combinators do with an empty array?
flashcards.back: `all` and `allSettled` fulfill with `[]`. `any` rejects with an `AggregateError`. `race` stays pending forever.
Always a promise. It fulfills with the returned value, or rejects with the error thrown inside.
Inside an `async` function, and at the top level of an ES module (ES2022). Anywhere else it is a `SyntaxError`.

flashcards.front: How do you run two awaited calls at the same time?
flashcards.back: Start both, then wait for both: `await Promise.all([a(), b()])`. Two `await` lines in a row run one after another.

flashcards.front: Which runs first: a promise `then` or `setTimeout(fn, 0)`?
flashcards.back: The `then` callback. All microtasks run before the next task, whatever order you set them up in.
Promise handlers (`then`, `catch`, `finally`), code after `await`, and `queueMicrotask`. `MutationObserver` callbacks too.

flashcards.front: How can you log every click on an element without changing code?
flashcards.back: In the Chrome DevTools console run `monitorEvents($0, 'click')` on the selected element. Stop with `unmonitorEvents($0)`.

flashcards.front: Why does a `var` loop with `setTimeout` log the same number?
flashcards.back: There is only one `var` variable, and the loop is done before the timers run. `let` makes a new variable for each turn.

flashcards.front: In a CommonJS Node script, which runs first: `process.nextTick` or a promise `then`?
flashcards.back: The `process.nextTick` callback. Node empties the next-tick queue before the promise microtask queue.

flashcards.front: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` or `setImmediate(fn)`: which runs first in Node?
flashcards.back: From the main script, the order is not fixed. Inside an I/O callback, `setImmediate` always runs first.

questions.q: What does it mean that JavaScript runs your code on a single thread?
options: Only one network request can be in flight at a time
Each timer must finish before the next line can run
The engine can never use any other thread at all
Only one piece of your code runs at any moment
questions.explain: One thread means one piece of your JavaScript runs at a time. Slow work like timers and I/O is handed off, and its callback waits its turn.
wrong: Many requests can be in flight; only your own code runs one piece at a time.
Code keeps running; timer callbacks wait in a queue until later.
Web Workers and Node worker threads exist. Your main code still runs one piece at a time.

questions.explain: A timer callback runs only after the current code is done, even with a 0 ms delay. So the two sync logs come first.
wrong: A 0 ms timer still waits until the current code has finished.
The timer callback still runs, just after the sync code.
Synchronous lines run in order, so 1 comes before 3.

questions.q: In the Node.js callback style, what is the first argument passed to a completion callback?
options: An error object, or `null` when the call worked
The result, with any `err` passed as the second argument
A `done` function to call when your own step is finished
The time in milliseconds that the call took to finish
questions.explain: Node reserves the first callback argument for an error. It is `null` or `undefined` when the operation worked, and the result follows.
wrong: Node puts the error first and the result second, not the other way round.
That is a pattern in some libraries, not the Node completion callback.
Node does not pass timing data to completion callbacks.

questions.q: What happens when this Node.js script runs?
options: `caught` is logged first, and then `done` is logged
`done` is logged, then the error is uncaught
questions.explain: `try...catch` only catches errors thrown while it is running. The callback runs later, after the `try` is gone, so the error is uncaught.
wrong: The `try` block finished long before the timer callback threw.
The `catch` block is no longer active when the callback runs.
Nothing is thrown inside the `try` block itself, so `catch` never runs.

questions.q: A developer has five nested callbacks. Each step needs the result of the step before. Which two changes flatten the code and keep the order? (Choose 2)
options: Make each step return a promise and chain the steps with `then`
Wrap all five calls together in one big `try...catch` block
Make the steps return promises and `await` each one in an `async` function
Call all five functions at once so none of them needs a callback
Replace every callback with a call to `setTimeout(step, 0)`
questions.explain: Promises and `async`/`await` were made to replace nested callbacks. A `then` chain or a row of `await` lines keeps the order without the nesting.
wrong: It flattens nothing, and it can't catch errors thrown in later callbacks.
Each step needs the last result, so they can't all start at once.
That only delays each step; results still need to be passed along.

questions.q: Which two calls start work that finishes later, after the current code? (Choose 2)
questions.explain: Timers and Node's callback I/O are asynchronous: their callbacks run later. Array methods and `JSON.parse` are synchronous.
wrong: `map` calls `fn` for each item right away, before it returns.
`JSON.parse` does its work at once and returns the result.
`forEach` calls `fn` for each item right away, in order.

questions.explain: A callback is not async by itself. `getUser` calls it at once, so it runs between the two sync logs.
wrong: `getUser` calls the callback straight away, not later.
`getUser` runs only after `start` is logged.
The callback is called, so `Ada` is logged.

options: Only `loop done`, because the timer missed its slot
Either order, depending on how fast the CPU is
questions.explain: JavaScript runs each job to completion. The timer is due after 0 ms, but it waits until the busy loop and the last log are done.
wrong: A callback can't interrupt running code (run-to-completion).
A late timer still runs; it just runs late.
The order is fixed: running code always finishes first.

questions.q: The config file is sometimes missing, and the app then crashes inside `JSON.parse`. What is the best fix?
options: Wrap the `fs.readFile(...)` call in a `try...catch` block
Pass a second callback to `fs.readFile` just for errors
Check `err` first and return early when it is set
Listen for an `'error'` event on the `fs` module
questions.explain: In an error-first callback the error arrives as the first argument. Check `err` before using `text`, and stop there if it is set.
wrong: The callback runs later, and the read error is passed in, not thrown.
`fs.readFile` takes one callback; the error is its first argument.
`fs` is not an event emitter; callback errors arrive as `err`.

questions.q: Callers of `load` complain that their callback sometimes runs before `load` returns and sometimes after. What is the problem, and the usual fix?
options: The cache leaks memory; switch to a `WeakMap` keyed by each file name
`readFile` runs twice for each key; put `await` before `fs.readFile`
`cb` runs twice per call; add a `return` after the line `cb(data)`
`cb` is sometimes called sync; defer that call with `queueMicrotask`
questions.explain: An API should be always sync or always async. The cached path calls `cb` at once, so defer it with `queueMicrotask` or `process.nextTick`.
wrong: A `WeakMap` can't take strings as keys, and memory isn't the issue.
`await` on a non-promise call changes nothing about the callback.
Each path calls `cb` once; the problem is when, not how often.

questions.explain: Only callbacks handed to async APIs run later. `now` calls its callback at once; `later` puts it in the timer queue.
wrong: `later` defers its callback with a timer, so `a` waits.
`now` calls its callback at once, before `c` is logged.
The timer callback still runs, after all the sync code.

questions.q: Which two statements about run-to-completion in JavaScript are true? (Choose 2)
options: A timer callback never starts while other code is still running
A timer callback can break into a loop once its delay has passed
Each callback gets a new thread so that it can run straight away
A long loop delays every timer and click handler that is due
`setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs `fn` before the line that comes after it
questions.explain: Each job runs to the end before the next one starts. So a busy loop holds up every waiting callback, even ones that are already due.
wrong: Callbacks wait for the running code to finish; nothing interrupts it.
Callbacks run on the same main thread, one at a time.
A 0 ms timer still waits until the current code finishes.

questions.q: A Node.js developer wants a promise version of the error-first `fs.readFile`. Which built-in tool turns it into a function that returns a promise?
questions.explain: `util.promisify` takes an error-first callback function and returns one that returns a promise. Node also has `fs.promises` built in.
wrong: That gives a promise of the function itself; it never reads a file.
`fs.readFile` would get `resolve` and `reject` as its path and options.
Functions have no `then` method.

questions.q: Which list names the three states of a promise?
questions.explain: A promise starts pending, then becomes fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. Fulfilled or rejected is called settled.
wrong: These are not promise states; "in progress" is not a state at all.
Open and closed are not promise states.
Settled means fulfilled or rejected; it is not a third state.

questions.explain: A promise settles only once. After `resolve('ok')`, the later `reject` call does nothing.
wrong: The promise was already fulfilled, so the `reject` call is ignored.
A promise settles once; only one handler runs.
Extra `resolve` or `reject` calls are silently ignored.

questions.q: Which call does the same as `promise.catch(handle)`?
questions.explain: `catch(fn)` is a short way to write `then(undefined, fn)`. It only handles rejections.
wrong: The first `then` argument handles fulfillment, not rejection.
`finally` runs either way and doesn't receive the error.
That runs `handle` with good values and ignores errors.

questions.explain: The next `then` gets whatever the handler returns. An arrow function with braces and no `return` returns `undefined`.
wrong: The first handler works out `n * 2` but never returns it.
The next `then` gets what the handler returned, not the original value.
Nothing reads a property of `undefined`, so no error is thrown.

questions.explain: A throw rejects the chain, so it skips to the next `catch`. After `catch` handles it, the chain is fulfilled again and `end` runs.
wrong: A thrown error skips the `then` handlers until a `catch`.
`catch` returns a fulfilled promise, so the last `then` still runs.
The error is not swallowed; it skips `two` and reaches `catch`.

questions.explain: `finally` passes the earlier result through unchanged. A normal value returned from its callback is ignored.
wrong: A normal return value from `finally` is ignored.
`finally` passes the earlier value through.
